q.t: In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, where are most minor criminal cases dealt with?
q.e: In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, most minor criminal cases are dealt with in a Magistrates' Court. In Scotland, minor criminal offences go to a Justice of the Peace Court.
o: In a Magistrates' Court
In a Crown Court
In a Justice of the Peace Court
In a County Court

q.t: Which of these statements is correct?
q.e: In England, Wales and Scotland magistrates and Justices of the Peace usually work unpaid and do not need legal qualifications. In Northern Ireland, cases are heard by a District Judge or Deputy District Judge, who is legally qualified and paid.
o: In Northern Ireland minor criminal cases are heard by a paid, legally qualified District Judge
In Northern Ireland minor criminal cases are heard by unpaid magistrates with no legal qualifications

q.t: In Scotland, where are the most serious cases, such as murder, heard?
q.e: In Scotland, serious cases are heard in a Sheriff Court with either a sheriff or a sheriff with a jury. The most serious cases in Scotland, such as murder, are heard at a High Court with a judge and jury.
o: At a High Court, with a judge and jury
In a Justice of the Peace Court
In a Crown Court
In the Court of Session

q.t: How many members does a jury have in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, and how many in Scotland?
q.e: A jury is made up of members of the public chosen at random from the local electoral register. In England, Wales and Northern Ireland a jury has 12 members, and in Scotland a jury has 15 members.
o: 12 in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, and 15 in Scotland
15 in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, and 12 in Scotland
12 everywhere in the UK
10 in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, and 12 in Scotland

q.t: Which third verdict is possible in Scotland?
q.e: The jury has to listen to the evidence presented at the trial and then decide a verdict of 'guilty' or 'not guilty' based on what they have heard. In Scotland, a third verdict of 'not proven' is also possible.
o: Not proven
Not guilty by reason of doubt
Case dismissed
No case to answer

q.t: If a jury finds a defendant guilty, who decides the penalty?
q.e: The jury has to listen to the evidence presented at the trial and then decide a verdict of 'guilty' or 'not guilty'. If the jury finds a defendant guilty, the judge decides on the penalty.
o: The judge
The jury
The police
The magistrates

q.t: From where is a jury chosen?
q.e: A jury is made up of members of the public chosen at random from the local electoral register. Everyone who is summoned to do jury service must do it unless they are not eligible or they provide a good reason to be excused.
o: At random from the local electoral register
From a list kept by the police
From volunteers who apply to the court
From members of the local council

q.t: In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, cases involving an accused person of what age are normally heard in a Youth Court?
q.e: In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, if an accused person is aged 10 to 17, the case is normally heard in a Youth Court in front of up to three specially trained magistrates or a District Judge.
o: Aged 10 to 17
Aged 14 to 17
Aged 10 to 21
Aged 16 to 18

q.t: Which TWO of these are true of Youth Courts?
q.e: The parents or carers of the young person are expected to attend the hearing. Members of the public are not allowed in Youth Courts, and the name or photographs of the accused young person cannot be published in newspapers or used by the media.
o: Members of the public are not allowed in
The young person cannot be named in newspapers
A jury of 12 decides the verdict
Hearings are always broadcast on television

q.t: What system is used in Scotland to deal with children and young people who have committed an offence?
q.e: In Scotland a system called the Children's Hearings System is used to deal with children and young people who have committed an offence. Northern Ireland has a system of youth conferencing.
o: The Children's Hearings System
Youth conferencing
The Youth Court
The Justice of the Peace Court

q.t: Which court in Scotland deals with most of the civil matters handled by County Courts elsewhere?
q.e: County Courts deal with a wide range of civil disputes. These include people trying to get back money that is owed to them, cases involving personal injury, family matters, breaches of contract, and divorce. In Scotland, most of these matters are dealt with in the Sheriff Court.
o: The Sheriff Court
The Court of Session
The High Court
The Justice of the Peace Court

q.t: Where are more serious civil cases dealt with in Scotland?
q.e: More serious civil cases, for example when a large amount of compensation is being claimed, are dealt with in the High Court in England, Wales and Northern Ireland. In Scotland, they are dealt with in the Court of Session in Edinburgh.
o: In the Court of Session, in Edinburgh
In the High Court, in Edinburgh
In the Sheriff Court
In a Crown Court

q.t: What are the small claims limits in England and Wales, and in Scotland and Northern Ireland?
q.e: The small claims procedure is an informal way of helping people to settle minor disputes without spending a lot of time and money using a lawyer. This procedure is used for claims of less than £10,000 in England and Wales and £5,000 in Scotland and Northern Ireland.
o: Less than £10,000 in England and Wales, and £5,000 in Scotland and Northern Ireland
Less than £5,000 in England and Wales, and £10,000 in Scotland and Northern Ireland
Less than £10,000 everywhere in the UK
Less than £1,000 in England and Wales, and £5,000 in Scotland

q.t: Where is a small claims hearing held?
q.e: The hearing is held in front of a judge in an ordinary room, and people from both sides of the dispute sit around a table. Small claims can also be issued online through Money Claims Online.
o: In front of a judge in an ordinary room, with both sides around a table
In a Crown Court in front of a jury
In the House of Lords
In a police station

q.t: What do solicitors do?
q.e: Solicitors are trained lawyers who give advice on legal matters, take action for their clients and represent their clients in court. Solicitors' charges are usually based on how much time they spend on a case.
o: Give legal advice, act for clients and represent them in court
Decide the verdict in criminal cases
Set the sentence when a person is found guilty
Appoint judges to the courts

q.t:
Is the statement below TRUE or FALSE?
If judges find that a public body is not respecting someone's legal rights, they can order that body to change its practices and pay compensation.
q.e: Judges are responsible for interpreting the law and ensuring that trials are conducted fairly. If judges find that a public body is not respecting someone's legal rights, they can order that body to change its practices and/or pay compensation.
o: TRUE
FALSE

q.t: If judges decide that the actions of the government are illegal, what must the government do?
q.e: Sometimes the actions of the government are claimed to be illegal. If the judges agree, then the government must either change its policies or ask Parliament to change the law.
o: Change its policies or ask Parliament to change the law
Dismiss the judges concerned
Hold a General Election
Refer the matter to the monarch

q.t: Which of these is NOT given in the handbook as an example of criminal law?
q.e: Examples of criminal laws are carrying a weapon, drugs, racial crime, selling tobacco to those under 18, smoking in public places, buying alcohol for those under 18, and drinking in public where there are alcohol-free zones. Housing disputes between landlords and tenants are an example of civil law.
o: A dispute between a landlord and a tenant over repairs
Carrying a knife for self-defence
Selling cigarettes to a person aged under 18
Causing distress to someone because of their religion

q.t: Who leads the separate police forces in the UK, and to whom are they answerable?
q.e: The police are organised into a number of separate police forces headed by Chief Constables. They are independent of the government.
o: Chief Constables, and the forces are independent of the government
The Home Secretary, who directs each force
Police and Crime Commissioners, who are appointed by the Prime Minister
Local magistrates, who direct each force

q.t: What do PCSOs usually do?
q.e: Police officers are supported by police community support officers (PCSOs). PCSOs have different roles according to the area but usually patrol the streets, work with the public, and support police officers at crime scenes and major events.
o: Patrol the streets, work with the public and support officers at crime scenes
Decide which cases go to court
Set the local policing budget
Appoint the Chief Constable

q.t: Which TWO independent bodies can receive complaints about the police?
q.e: Complaints can also be made to an independent body: the Independent Police Complaints Commission in England and Wales, the Police Complaints Commissioner for Scotland or the Police Ombudsman for Northern Ireland.
o: The Police Complaints Commissioner for Scotland
The Police Ombudsman for Northern Ireland
The Citizens Advice Bureau
The Equality and Human Rights Commission

q.t: What is meant by extremism in the handbook?
q.e: It is important that all citizens feel safe. This includes feeling safe from all kinds of extremism, vocal or active opposition to fundamental British values, including religious extremism and far-right extremism.
o: Vocal or active opposition to fundamental British values
Any strong political opinion
Membership of a pressure group
Voting for a small political party

q.t: If someone tries to recruit you to an extremist cause, who should you report it to?
q.e: All terrorist groups try to radicalise and recruit people to their cause. If you think someone is trying to persuade you to join an extremist or terrorist cause, you should notify your local police force.
o: Your local police force
The Citizens Advice Bureau
Your local council
The Independent Police Complaints Commission

q.t:
Is the statement below TRUE or FALSE?
Every person in the UK receives equal treatment under the law.
q.e: Every person in the UK receives equal treatment under the law. This means that the law applies in the same way to everyone, no matter who they are or where they are from.
o: TRUE
FALSE
